Parent: "That's right. On Sundays, Spoon goes to visit his Aunt Silver. He has to be on his very best behavior there. She's very fancy and proper. 'Goodbye, Darling. Ta-ta!' Look, what's he wearing?"

Parent: "Yeah. A tie. At bedtime, Spoon likes to hear the story about his adventurous great-grandmother who fell in love with a dish and ran off to a distant island. Do you ever listen to stories at night? Yeah? Lately though, Spoon had been feeling..."

Parent: "What's wrong?" Asked his mother, "You look a bit bent out of shape."
Child: "Nothing," mumbled Spoon. But do you think something is really wrong?"

Parent: Let's find out. "It's just that, I don't know, all my friends have it so much better than me. Like Knife. Knife is so lucky. He gets to cut." Where's Knife? What else can Knife do, do you think?
Child: (continues to point at the screen)

Parent: You want to find out on the next page?
Child: (interacts with the tablet to flip the page)
Child: (gestures towards the screen, looking at it)
Child: Yeah, that's right. "He gets to spread. I never get to cut or spread." "Yes, Knife is pretty spiffy that way, isn't he?"
Child: Yes, he does. No, no, this guy gets to cut sometimes.
Parent: Does the spoon cut sometimes?
Child: (gestures with hand as if holding a spoon)
Child: Yeah, because you have a spoon right here and right here, you [inaudible 00:03:26] then cut with the spoon accidentally.

Parent: On accident? Yeah. That could happen, I guess. "And Fork. Fork is so lucky. She gets to go practically everywhere. I bet she never goes stir crazy like I do." "Fork does get out and make herself useful, doesn't she?"
Child: (continues observing the screen) What's Fork doing in all of those?
Parent: Look, this is a grill and do you see what's cooking there?
Child: (continues looking at the screen, touches tablet briefly)
Parent: Fork [inaudible 00:03:56], Fork is going to die.

Parent: I don't think so. Look at that. Can we look at it again?
Parent: No. Okay. "And Chopsticks. They are so lucky. Everyone thinks they're really cool and exotic. No one thinks I'm cool or exotic." What do the chopsticks do?
Parent: They do [shoe shoe 00:04:12]. Mm-hmm (affirmative). "Those Chopsticks are something else, aren't they?" They are pretty great, huh?
Child: (nods, continues to look at the tablet, finger on chin)
Parent: "Meanwhile, if only Spoon knew what his friends were saying at that very minute. Cling, clang, bang. Let's find out what they were saying. What do you think they're saying about Spoon?"
Child: (leans in and looks at the tablet)

Parent: "Mm-hmm (affirmative), that's right. "Spoon is so lucky," said Knife. Thank you. "He's so fun and easygoing. Everyone's so serious with me, no one's ever allowed to be silly with me like they are with spoon." Look, he's having so much fun. They're thinking of how he does that. Let's see what else Spoon can do. 'Spoon is so lucky,' said Fork, 'He gets to measure stuff. No one ever does that with me.'"
Parent: "But you do get peanut butter on you, and you get peanut butter on you because [inaudible 00:05:14] peanut butter fork, peanut butter spoon, peanut butter knife."
Child: (smiling and looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Oh, wow. 'Spoon is so lucky,' said Chopsticks. 'He can go places by himself. We could never function apart.' That night after bedtime stories, Spoon's mom turned off the lights, tucked him in and said..."

Parent: "I don't know. Let's find out. 'You know, Spoon, I wonder if you realize just how lucky you are. Your friends will never know the joy of diving headfirst into a bowl of ice-cream. They'll never know what it feels like to cling against the side of a cereal bowl. They'll never be able to twirl around in a mug or relax in a hot cup of tea.' What do you think? Is that looking fun?"
Child: (leaning on the table, looking at the tablet)
Child: (leans in closer to the tablet, still focused)
Parent: "Spoon hadn't thought of it that way before. He lay awake in bed for a long time. His mind was racing, he felt so alive."
Child: (keeps looking at the tablet, slightly tilting his head)
Parent: "There was only one thing to do. Then he says here, 'I can't sleep.' They said, 'Come snuggle, come Spoon.'"
Parent: "And so, he did. What's he doing?"
Parent: "Yep. 'Sweet dreams,' and look at all of the things. Do you see what he's dreaming of?"
Child: (looks at parent, waiting for a response)
Parent: "Okay, so that one looks like a milkshake, right? And some pie and another cake and then ice-cream and another dessert. What do people use to eat those?"
Parent: "Yeah. So, that's the first page and then if you want to go... Yeah."
Parent: "Do you want to read any of these ones? Which one is that one?"

Parent: "Then we can turn the next page. The cow jumping over the moon. There are three little bears sitting on chairs. Where's that one?"
Parent: "Yeah. And two little kittens. Where are the two little kittens?"

Parent: "Harold. Mm-hmm (affirmative). One evening after thinking over it for sometime, Harold decided to go for a walk in the moonlight. He made a long straight path so he wouldn't get lost. Do you see it?"

Parent: "The moon sailed along with him. After he sailed long enough, Harold made land without much trouble. Because guess who's the one who draws the land?"

Parent: "Mm-hmm (affirmative). The sandy beach reminded Harold of picnics and the thought of picnics made him hungry. Do you think you would want to draw a picnic blanket too?"

Parent: "He hated to see so much delicious pie go to waste."
Parent: "What else could it be? It could be a giraffe. What else?"

Child: (smiling and looking at the parent) Mountain.

Parent: (nodding) Mm-hmm. If he went high enough, he thought he could see the window of his bedroom. He was tired and he felt he ought to be getting to bed. Do you think you would be tired after climbing a mountain?
Parent: (smiling) Yeah? He hoped he could see his bedroom window from the top of the mountain.

Parent: “Then suddenly, Harold remembered. He remembered where his bedroom window was when there was a moon. It was right around the moon. Then Harold made his bed. He got in it and he drew up the covers.”
